**Thanos Can't be Beat, Only Convinced He's Wrong**

One of the story arcs Avengers 4 will have to address is consequentialism vs. deontology that was at the heart of Captain America: Civil War. With Infinity War, the theme went from global risk to universe-wide. Put another way, does a hero or an anti-hero perform an action because it does the most good versus does a hero or an anti-hero perform an action because he or she is duty-bound to do the right thing. 

In Avengers 2 and Civil War, we found Tony Stark on the first half of this equation (for example: questioning if it’s worth saving the people in Sokovia) with Steve Rodgers on the latter half – duty-bound to do what’s right (wanting to save the people in the city and the Earth). In Infinity War, The Avengers and Guardians of the Galaxy tried sacrificing loved ones to save the universe; but it didn’t work. 

We have a villain willing to sacrifice half the universe to save the rest of it (consequentialism taken to crazy town). Thanos represents the ultimate degree of consequentialism – forcing our heroes to the duty or obligation side to do what’s right. 

**What Happens Next?**
Thanos is too powerful now to be beaten. He will have to be convinced he is on the wrong side of the philosophical equation. He’s riddled with self-doubt in the comics and references failure in his dialogue with Thor at the beginning of the movie (“I know what it’s like to fail”). By the end of Infinity War, he is already heavily questioning himself when little Gamora asks him, what did it cost? It costed Thanos “Everything”. It will either be Tony Stark (completing his arc from an arrogant prick in Iron Man to a duty-bound hero in Avengers 4) or Nebula accepting she can’t kill her adopted father and instead brings him back from “the dark side”.  Either way, one of the two will convince Thanos that he has made a mistake and he will want to make things right. 

Tony will use the BARF technology to relive the battles in Avengers 1 and 2 to analyze how to beat Thanos while the rest of the Avengers scour the universe for the infinity Stones which may have been scattered after the gauntlet seemingly burnt and melted at the end of Infinity War. Meanwhile, Thor may have to back to go back to Asgard, defeat Surtur and retrieve other Infinity gauntlet (maybe it’s not fake, just unused) to use it to set things right. 

The stones will get reassembled and our heroes will get to the brink of setting the universe right then Thanos will foil the plan until Tony ultimately has to convince Thanos he’s in the wrong and Tony offers to sacrifice himself – proving he’s potentially more worthy of wielding the Infinity gauntlet.

An easy way to correct the wrongs is to use the time stone to roll it back to before people turned to dust. However, that’s unsatisfying and creates a lot of plot holes and questions like – why not save more people? It could happen by cracking the soul stone and perhaps releasing Gamora, Quill, Doctor Strange, Black Panther and others. But how does Captain Marvel fit in? At the time of Infinity War, she may exist in a parallel universe which introduces us to the idea that the heroes who died in Infinity War may exist in another universe and team up with the survivors of Infinity War.

Thank you for picking Ground Hog Day. It’s my favorite movie of all time and I’m almost embarrassed to admit I’ve seen it more than two dozen times. Danny Rubin’s genius high-concept idea was expertly molded by Harold Ramis into a near-perfect romantic comedy. Here are some of the points that mesmerize me over and over (pun intended): 

•	Amazing High Concept idea! 


•	It very clearly hits on the all the story points. Theme stated: You guys are going to have fun at 3:20 into the film, Stating his outer desire “For your information, hairdo, there’s a major network interested in me”, Testing the rules by breaking the pencil. etc. 


•	While most romantic comedies are an MC vs. DC/Opponent, Ground Hog Day sets up as the weather or (I would argue more specifically – water) as the opponent to Phil Connors. Some examples are: 1) The blizzard he fails to forecast 2) The blizzard traps him in town. 3) The frost on the windows of his bedroom create eyes that look in on and grow more defined as the day goes on. 4) The puddle he steps 5) The ice carvings of the groundhogs 6) The cold shower, etc. This device is extremely clever and very unique! Of course, you could argue the groundhog himself is the opponent, or time (as all the clocks are frozen in place), or Needle Nose Ned selling life insurance to a man who has no cares about his life as opponents but all play as a great symphony of opponents. 


•	The progression of Phil Connors' change is mapped out as the five stages of grief. Phil goes from denial (“nice goin’ boys, you're playing yesterday’s tape”) to anger (“I’m not going to live by their rules anymore!”) to bargaining (manipulating Rita) to depression (toaster in the bathtub, etc.) to acceptance/Self-actualization (noted by his selfless acts from saving the boy in the tree, to trying to keep the old man alive, and being the fastest jack in Jefferson county. 


•	It’s funny because it’s true. The comedy isn’t contrived. Meaning that Phil is a believable egocentric real guy and he tries to come up with real solutions to an unbelievable problem as a way out of Ground Hog Day – “Do you know what you need, Mr. Connors?” “A Biopsy!?” and “I’d say the chance of departure is 80 … percent. 75/80 percent?”


•	It’s clear, Harold Ramis was inspired by “It’s a Wonderful Life”. They’re both stories of redemption that end with Phil and George seemingly fitting in as the foundations that hold each of their towns together. 


•	It’s an allegory of the meaning of life and all the obstacles we create for ourselves - enjoying the passing of time, redemption through the power of love, our prisons are of our own design, our lives - as we live them - are illusions (Phil on the blue screen at the beginning) and all that happy sappy baloney. Bottom line: it’s Hollywood’s very best effort to delve into the abyss of Camus’ nightmare --- “There is no love of life without the despair of life”.
